title: Alypius at the games (6.8)
hookLine: his friend swears he'll keep his eyes shut and is caught by the roar
tomorrow: who does the book send away, and never name?

cards: Thumb over the screen, scrolling fast past the fight video, promising yourself you won't watch. Then the comments explode. Augustine's friend Alypius made that promise in Rome, where he'd gone to study law.
Friends coming from dinner dragged him, laughing, to the gladiator shows, which he hated. You can drag my body there, he told them, but not my mind or my eyes. He sat down and shut his eyes.
Could he keep them shut when the whole arena roared?

teach.h: A DEEPER WOUND THAN THE FIGHTER'S.
teach.b: No. Someone fell in the fight, the crowd let out a huge shout, and curiosity won. He opened his eyes, sure he could look down on whatever he saw.
Augustine says he took a deeper wound in his soul than the fighter took in his body. He didn't turn away. He fixed his eyes, shouted, burned, and carried home a madness that drew him back again.
So why didn't his promise hold?

Augustine's answer is plain: Alypius trusted his own strength, when he should have trusted God. And he doesn't leave his friend there; God later pulled Alypius out, he says, and taught him that trust.
A neighbor tradition sees the same danger.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, pictures someone who lives looking for pleasures, senses unguarded: the tempter throws him down the way wind throws down a weak tree.
The one who guards the senses stands like a rocky mountain. Both say don't take the seat and count on your eyes. And one honest difference.
For Augustine, the strength that finally held was God's, not Alypius's own.

teach.h: GOD'S STRENGTH, OR SELF AS LORD.
teach.b: The Dhammapada puts the work in your own hands: self, it says, is the lord of self.
One danger, two maps for crossing it.

how: Catholic moral teaching speaks of avoiding the 'near occasion of sin': stepping away from places and situations known to pull a person in, rather than relying on willpower alone.

games.q: what does “alypius at the games” mean?
o: a friend who swore he wouldn't watch, then did
a friend who refused to go and stayed home
a champion who won the games in Rome

p: swore his eyes would stay shut
the guarded one stands like a mountain

s: willpower alone kept Alypius safe once he'd sat down
one roar and his eyes were open. Augustine says he trusted his own strength.
Augustine says God later pulled Alypius out
and taught him to trust not himself but God.
only Christians teach guarding what you let in
the Dhammapada pictures the guarded one standing like a rocky mountain.

games.q: your cousin swears he can go to the casino night with his friends and "just watch." what does Alypius's story say?
o: don't count on your eyes once you've taken the seat.
he'll be fine if his promise is strong enough.
go, and leave the moment it gets exciting.
games.why: Alypius said he'd be absent while present. one roar and he was shouting. the choice that mattered was the seat.

practice: Before the sit begins, do one small thing: put your phone face down across the room, or close the tab that tends to pull you in. That's the seat, moved.
Then sit with the space it leaves, and notice how the pull feels from farther away.

wordCard.voice: Alypius at the games. Augustine's friend swore his eyes would stay shut, trusted his own strength, and one roar did the rest.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the roar, which he didn't choose, though he chose the seat. Rest easy.
